status_legend.renewed_narrowed: Renewed with narrower permitted uses, added exclusions, or narrower covered class

exemptions.name: Filtering software block-lists
exemptions.summary: Circumvent TPMs on compilations of websites/Internet locations blocked by filtering software, to study or analyze the block-list contents.

2003.notes: Refined: 'lists of Internet locations blocked' replaces 'lists of websites blocked'

exemptions.evolution_notes: Granted in the very first §1201 rulemaking (2000) and renewed in 2003; dropped from 2006 onward. The original justification (filtering-software research) was overtaken by the broader debate over content filters.

exemptions.name: Literary works with malfunctioning/obsolete access controls
exemptions.summary: Circumvent broken or obsolete TPMs on literary works (incl. computer programs and databases) when the TPM no longer permits access due to malfunction, damage, or obsoleteness.
exemptions.evolution_notes: Single-cycle exemption (2000 only). The broad framing was replaced in 2003 by two narrower classes targeting the specific problems of obsolete dongles and obsolete formats.

exemptions.name: Obsolete dongles
exemptions.summary: Circumvent dongles (hardware TPMs) when the dongle has become obsolete because malfunctioning and no replacement is reasonably available.

partial_denials.topic: Dongle class expansion to broader incompatibilities/obsolete OS or hardware
partial_denials.reason_quote: That request was untimely. The purpose of the hearing, at a relatively late stage of the proceedings, is not to accept new proposals for exemptions or to entertain requests for expanded versions of exemptions that were proposed in a timely manner.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Renewed three cycles (2003 → 2006 → 2010). Disappears after 2010 as the legacy-dongle problem became obsolete in turn (most production software no longer used hardware dongles by the mid-2010s).

exemptions.name: Computer programs/games in obsolete formats
exemptions.summary: Circumvent TPMs on computer programs and video games distributed in formats requiring obsolete machines or systems as a condition of access. Refined in 2006 to focus on library/archive preservation.

2006.notes: Refined to library/archive preservation purposes — narrows the user class but retains the work class

exemptions.evolution_notes: Two cycles (2003, 2006). Library preservation of computer programs was effectively re-introduced in 2018 as a NEW separately-tracked class ('software-preservation-lams') with stricter eligibility criteria.

exemptions.name: Literary works (electronic) — accessibility (musical notation added 2021)
exemptions.summary: Circumvent TPMs that prevent enabling read-aloud functionality or interfere with screen readers / assistive technologies, for blind/disabled individuals or authorized entities under 17 U.S.C. 121. Expanded in 2021 to include previously published musical notation.

2021.notes: Adds 'previously published musical works that have been fixed in the form of text or notation'; terminology updated to 'eligible person' (post-Marrakesh)

exemptions.evolution_notes: Longest-running renewable exemption (eight consecutive cycles from 2003 to 2024). Carried forward essentially unchanged for 18 years; significantly expanded in 2021 by adding musical notation, then renewed unchanged in 2024.

exemptions.name: Motion pictures — captioning & audio description by educational disability services
exemptions.summary: Educational disability services may circumvent TPMs on lawfully acquired motion pictures (DVD/Blu-ray/digital) to add captions and audio description for students (2018), or for students, faculty, or staff (2021+) with disabilities.

2021.notes: Beneficiaries expanded from 'students with disabilities' to 'students, faculty, or staff with disabilities'; adds 'accessible version of sufficient quality' definition; adds explicit reuse permission; adds textbook-bundle scenario; price standard refined to 'fair market price'

exemptions.evolution_notes: Newer accessibility class focused on closed captions and audio description in educational settings. Notably expanded in 2021 to cover faculty/staff (not just students) and to allow institutional reuse of created accessible versions.

exemptions.name: Motion pictures — R&D of accessibility players (blind/deaf/HoH)
exemptions.summary: Circumvent CSS / online-distribution TPMs to enable research and development of accessibility-enhanced players (e.g., that integrate audio descriptions or captions inaccessibly delivered).
exemptions.evolution_notes: Single-cycle exemption (2012). Allowed research-and-development circumvention with a proviso that resulting player must not itself require circumvention. Not renewed in 2015, possibly because the resulting players did not require ongoing circumvention or the use case was overtaken by other accessibility solutions.

exemptions.name: Video games — accessibility input methods for physical disabilities
exemptions.summary: Circumvent TPMs on lawfully acquired video games running on a general-purpose computer, to allow a user with a physical disability to use input methods other than a standard keyboard or mouse.
exemptions.evolution_notes: Single-cycle exemption (2021 only). Did NOT carry forward into 2024 because no renewal petition was filed (2024 Final Rule [PAGE 2] n.21).

exemptions.name: Motion pictures — short clips for criticism, comment, & educational uses
exemptions.summary: Circumvent CSS / AACS / digital-distribution TPMs to make short clips of motion pictures for criticism, comment, documentary filmmaking, noncommercial videos, e-book film analysis, and educational uses. Scope of users and uses has been heavily restructured across cycles.

2006.notes: Originally limited to film and media studies professors compiling classroom clips from DVDs

2010.notes: Expanded to three user categories: college/university educators; documentary filmmakers; noncommercial video creators

2012.notes: Restructured into 4 sub-classes: DVD/CSS+full-circ, online+full-circ, DVD/CSS+screen-cap, online+screen-cap. Added K-12 educators; added multimedia e-books

partial_denials.topic: Short clip circumvention for fictional filmmakers
partial_denials.reason_quote: The Register therefore concluded, on the record before her, that fictional filmmakers had failed to establish that the uses in which they sought to engage were likely to be noninfringing.

2015.notes: Consolidated back into single class with 8 enumerated sub-uses; added Blu-ray/AACS; added MOOCs; added K-12 students (screen-cap only); added digital/media-literacy programs

2018.notes: Adds parody and biographical/historically-significant uses to documentary-filmmaking branch; allows K-12 students (under educator supervision) to use full circumvention

2021.notes: Adds 'employees acting at the direction of faculty for the purpose of teaching a course' to both higher-ed and MOOC subparts

partial_denials.topic: Proposed Class 1 — OTW rewrite of noncommercial-videos subpart (no substantive change requested)
partial_denials.reason_quote: The Office received no comments in support of the proposal, no requests from OTW or other parties to participate in the public hearings, and no other evidence in support of the proposal. ... The Register does not recommend the expansion proposed as Class 1, which does not include substantive changes.

partial_denials.topic: Proposed Class 2 — MOOC expansion to for-profit / unaccredited educational entities
partial_denials.reason_quote: The Register finds that the record lacks support to expand the existing exemption to for-profit and/or unaccredited educational entities. She therefore does not recommend adopting the proposed exemption.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Granted in every cycle since 2006 (seven consecutive cycles). Each renewal has been an expansion — new user categories, source formats, or use cases — making this the single most consistently broadened exemption in §1201 history. 2012 partial denial: fictional filmmaker uses (clip circumvention specifically for fictional commercial films) was denied even as the broader class was expanded. 2024 partial denials: OTW's proposed reformatting of the noncommercial-videos subpart and a proposed MOOC-subpart expansion to for-profit/unaccredited educational entities were both denied.

exemptions.name: Space-shifting / format-shifting (audiovisual, musical, literary)
exemptions.summary: Recurring proposal: permit users to shift lawfully-acquired works (DVDs, CDs, e-books, streaming media) to alternative devices, formats, or platforms for personal use. Repeatedly DENIED across cycles, primarily because the Register has not found space-shifting / format-shifting to be a noninfringing use under existing fair-use law.

2000.reason_quote: any harm caused by the existence of access control measures used in DVDs can be avoided by obtaining a copy of the work in analog format.

2003.reason_quote: Commenters who believe that users should be able to 'space-shift' any work they purchase ... did not make a persuasive case that such 'space-shifting,' involving reproduction of the work, is a noninfringing use.

2006.reason_quote: these commenters uniformly failed to cite legal precedent that establishes that such space-shifting is, in fact, a noninfringing use.

2010.reason_quote: Mere consumer inconvenience is not sufficient to support the designation of a class of works.

2012.reason_quote: The Register concluded that proponents had failed to establish that the prohibition on circumvention is imposing an adverse impact on noninfringing uses and declined to recommend the requested exemptions for space shifting.

2015.reason_quote: the law of fair use, as it stands today, does not sanction broad-based space-shifting or format-shifting.

2018.reason_quote: the Acting Register found no basis to depart from the fair use analysis and ultimate conclusion reached in the 2015 proceeding, where the Register was unable to determine that the proposed uses were noninfringing.

2021.reason_quote: Petitioner failed to provide legal arguments or evidence to demonstrate that space-shifting is a noninfringing use.

exemptions.evolution_notes: The most-denied proposal in §1201 history: petitioned in essentially every cycle from 2000 to 2021 and consistently denied. The Register's position has been stable: in the absence of fair-use precedent recognizing space-shifting as noninfringing, §1201 cannot create one. Not proposed in 2024.

exemptions.name: DVD region coding & OS-tethered playback (Linux DVD)
exemptions.summary: Recurring proposal: permit circumvention of CSS to play DVDs on Linux or non-licensed platforms, or to bypass region coding. Repeatedly DENIED — Register has found alternative platforms / analog copies / region-free players are available.

2000.reason_quote: the inability to play a DVD on a particular device or with a particular operating system is simply a matter of preference and inconvenience.

2003.reason_quote: Because such consumers have a number of options that will permit them to view such region coded DVDs, the need for an exemption that would permit circumvention of region coding has not been demonstrated.

2006.reason_quote: Region coding imposes, at most, an inconvenience rather than actual or likely harm.

2010.reason_quote: Similar classes ... have been requested and denied in the past three rulemakings ... CSS-compatible DVD players are in fact available for some Linux systems.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Petitioned in four consecutive cycles (2000-2010) and denied every time. Stopped being petitioned after 2010 — Linux DVD playback was effectively solved at the technical level (CSS-compatible players became broadly available) and region-coding concerns faded with streaming.

exemptions.name: Backup copies of optical media (DVDs/CDs)
exemptions.summary: Petition to permit users to make backup copies of lawfully-acquired DVDs and CDs in case of physical damage. DENIED in 2003 and 2006: making backup copies of these media was not shown to be a noninfringing use.

2003.reason_quote: The Register concludes that the proponents have not made the case with respect to fragility of DVDs, nor have they shown that the making of backup copies of DVDs is a noninfringing use.

2006.reason_quote: the proponents offered no legal arguments in support of the proposition that the making of backup copies is noninfringing, and the Register is aware of no authority (apart from section 117 of the Copyright Act, which relates to computer programs) in support of that notion.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Closely related to space-shifting (the underlying fair-use issue). After two denials, the topic stopped being proposed.

exemptions.name: Broadcast flag circumvention
exemptions.summary: Petition to permit circumvention of an FCC-mandated broadcast flag that would restrict downstream recording of TV/radio broadcasts. DENIED in 2003, 2006, and 2010 — initially because the broadcast flag was speculative; later because the FCC mandate had been struck down by the courts and was no longer a live concern.

2003.reason_quote: The 'limited purpose' for which the broadcast monitors seek an exemption does not appear to constitute a noninfringing use. Moreover, the broadcast monitors' fears relating to the broadcast flag, which at this point is simply a proposal before another federal agency, are speculative.

2006.reason_quote: there is currently no broadcast flag mandate for either television or radio broadcasts and whether such a mandate will exist within the next three years is a matter of speculation.

2010.reason_quote: There is no broadcast flag mandate for digital television broadcasts in effect, and it is highly speculative as to whether broadcasters and copyright owners will work to implement measures to restrict consumer recording privileges in the new DTV era.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Tracks a particular regulatory fight from the 2000s. The FCC broadcast-flag rule was struck down by the D.C. Circuit in American Library Ass'n v. FCC (2005), and the topic faded after 2010.

exemptions.name: HDCP / HDMI / Blu-ray Image Constraint Token down-conversion
exemptions.summary: Petition to permit circumvention of HDCP/HDMI content-protection or Blu-ray Image Constraint Token (ICT) to obtain full-resolution playback or recording. DENIED in 2010 and 2018 — insufficient evidence of active use of these restrictions on Blu-ray/HDMI streams.

2010.reason_quote: He has not provided evidence that ICTs are currently being used on Blu-ray discs to restrict users from accessing the highest resolution format offered by Blu-ray discs.

2018.reason_quote: The record lacked the requisite detail and legal support for the Acting Register to conclude that the proposed uses are or are not likely to be noninfringing; the Acting Register also concluded that the proposed exemption was overly broad and that the request was an individual case of de minimis impact.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Two non-consecutive denials. Distinct from the granted motion-pictures-clips class because the HDCP/HDMI proposal would permit full-resolution recording (not just short clips for criticism).

exemptions.name: Livestream recording (audiovisual works)
exemptions.summary: Proposal to permit circumvention of HTTP Live Streaming TPMs to record audiovisual works originating as livestreams. DENIED in 2021 on procedural grounds — petitioner provided no legal arguments or evidence and did not participate in hearings.

2021.reason_quote: Petitioner did not provide legal arguments or evidence to support its petition and did not participate in the public hearings.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Single-cycle procedural denial. Not re-petitioned in 2024.

exemptions.name: Motion picture clips in text messages
exemptions.summary: Proposal to permit circumvention to enable sending short motion-picture clips in text messages. DENIED in 2021 as a de minimis showing — petitioner did not explain how the proposed uses were noninfringing or why an exemption was necessary.

2021.reason_quote: due to the de minimis showing provided by proponents, the Register does not recommend the adoption of an exemption for proposed Class 2.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Single-cycle de minimis denial.

exemptions.name: Copy-protected CDs & game-disc DRM (SecuROM/StarForce)
exemptions.summary: Petitions for circumvention of TPMs on audio CDs that block playback on certain devices (2003) and of computer-game copy-protection systems like SecuROM and StarForce (2006). DENIED for lack of evidence of active deployment and adverse effects.

2003.reason_quote: thus far the deployment of CDs protected by any technological measures in the United States has been minimal.

2006.reason_quote: The commenter did not present any evidence that the adverse effect articulated is the result of an access control.

exemptions.evolution_notes: The Sony rootkit incident later got its own targeted GRANTED exemption in 2006 (cd-security-testing-2006), but the general 'copy-protected CD' petitions for users were denied. Combined into one row because both are about consumer-side CD/game-disc TPMs.

exemptions.name: Motion pictures — TDM research at nonprofit higher-ed
exemptions.summary: Researchers at nonprofit higher-ed institutions may circumvent TPMs on lawfully acquired motion pictures to perform TDM research on a corpus, subject to security conditions and access controls.

2024.notes: Permitted viewing standard broadened from 'verification of research findings' to 'conduct TDM research or teaching'; adds trade-association disclosure right; adds explicit secure-connections + authenticated-credentials requirement

exemptions.evolution_notes: Two cycles (2021, 2024). 2024 expansion broadens what TDM researchers may do with the corpus content during their work, but tightens security/access requirements.

exemptions.name: Literary works — TDM research at nonprofit higher-ed
exemptions.summary: Researchers at nonprofit higher-ed institutions may circumvent TPMs on lawfully acquired electronically distributed literary works to perform TDM research on a corpus, subject to security conditions.

2024.notes: Same expansions as motion-pictures-tdm; explicitly excludes computer programs and TDM-purpose compilations from coverage

exemptions.evolution_notes: Sibling class to motion-pictures-tdm. Excludes computer programs (which would otherwise be a confounding category) and excludes compilations compiled specifically for TDM purposes (to prevent gaming the exemption).

exemptions.name: Video games on PCs — security research (2010-only)
exemptions.summary: Circumvent TPMs on lawfully acquired video games when used on personal computers, for good-faith testing/investigation/correction of security flaws, with conditions on use of derived information.
exemptions.evolution_notes: Single-cycle predecessor (2010) to the more general security-research class established in 2015. Tracked separately because its scope (video games on PCs only) was substantively narrower.

exemptions.name: Good-faith security research (general)
exemptions.summary: Researchers may circumvent TPMs on lawfully acquired devices/machines (and on computers/systems/networks with owner authorization) solely for good-faith security research, with conditions on the research environment and use of derived information.

2010.reason_quote: Halderman did not present any evidence that the prohibition on circumvention is adversely affecting or is likely, in the next three years, to adversely affect the ability to engage in noninfringing uses of sound recordings or audiovisual works, or of literary works except to the extent that video games may be considered, in part, to constitute audiovisual works.
2010.notes: Halderman's broader security-testing class (covering sound recordings, audiovisual works, and non-game literary works) was DENIED as evidence-insufficient; only the narrow video-game-PC subset was granted that cycle as 2010 (b)(4) (tracked under id 'video-game-security-research-2010'). This is the conceptual precursor to the 2015 general security-research class.

2015.notes: Initially limited to 3 device classes (consumer devices incl. voting machines; motorized land vehicles; implanted medical devices); 12-month delayed effective date

2018.notes: Device-class limitation removed; added coverage for computers/systems/networks with owner authorization; 12-month delay dropped

2021.notes: CFAA-non-violation precondition dropped — exemption no longer denied to researchers who incidentally violate CFAA; instead, separate liability under other laws remains possible

exemptions.evolution_notes: One of the most-expanded exemptions. Each renewal cycle from 2015 to 2021 substantively broadened the scope — from a 3-device-class list with a delay to general coverage of any device/system/network with owner authorization, free of CFAA-violation preconditions. 2024 stabilized.

exemptions.name: Sound recordings on CDs with security-flaw TPMs — 'Sony rootkit' testing
exemptions.summary: Circumvent TPMs on audio CDs that create security vulnerabilities or expose the protected work to unintended risks (the 'Sony rootkit' exemption), for the sole purpose of investigating and correcting those security flaws.
exemptions.evolution_notes: Single-cycle exemption directly responding to the 2005 Sony BMG rootkit incident. The specific audio-CD TPM-with-security-flaw use case became historical as the music industry abandoned CD-level TPMs.

exemptions.name: Generative AI trustworthiness research
exemptions.summary: Proposal to permit circumvention to enable trustworthiness research on generative AI systems (e.g., investigating bias, hallucination, safety). DENIED in 2024 — Register found the proponents' concerns arise from third-party online-platform terms of service, not from §1201, so a §1201 exemption would not address them.

2024.reason_quote: She finds, however, that the adverse effects identified by proponents arise from third-party control of online platforms rather than the operation of section 1201, so that an exemption would not ameliorate their concerns.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Newest denial. Notable because the Register's reasoning was structural (the harm arises from ToS, not from §1201) rather than evidentiary — i.e., even a perfect record would not have changed the outcome.

exemptions.name: Encryption research (broader than §1201(g))
exemptions.summary: Proposal to broaden the encryption-research exemption beyond §1201(g)'s statutory carve-out (e.g., to research on data files, password recovery, PII). DENIED in 2000 and 2003 — the Register held that 'encryption research' is defined by purpose/use, not by a class of works.

2000.reason_quote: an exemption for encryption research is not focused on a class of works.

2003.reason_quote: In some cases, the commenters failed to explain why the existing exemptions are insufficient. Most commenters also failed to provide specific examples of problems leading to the alleged need for an exemption.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Subsumed in practice by the broad good-faith security-research class first granted in 2015 (and progressively expanded). Encryption-research-specific petitions stopped after 2003.

exemptions.name: Reverse engineering for interoperability (broader than §1201(f))
exemptions.summary: Proposal to broaden the reverse-engineering exemption beyond §1201(f)'s statutory carve-out (e.g., to printer toner remanufacturing, broader interoperability). DENIED in 2000 and 2003 — substantive: defined by purpose, not by class of works; and §1201(f) was held adequate.

2000.reason_quote: A 'class of works' cannot be defined simply in terms of the purpose for which circumvention is desired.

2003.reason_quote: The Register concludes that an existing exemption in section 1201(f) addresses the concerns of remanufacturers, making an exemption under section 1201(a)(1)(D) unnecessary.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Conceptually overlaps with the granted FOSS license-investigation class (2021) and with various jailbreaking/interoperability classes. The original broad reverse-engineering framing has not been re-petitioned since 2003.

exemptions.name: Forensic investigator evidence collection
exemptions.summary: Proposal to permit forensic investigators to circumvent TPMs to collect digital evidence. DENIED in 2010 — proponent failed to describe the proposed class of works or provide compelling evidence of adverse effects.

2010.reason_quote: Pannenborg failed to intelligibly describe the nature of authorship of the proposed class of works.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Single-cycle denial. Has not been re-petitioned.

exemptions.name: Motion pictures (DVD/Blu-ray) — preservation by LAMs
exemptions.summary: Eligible LAMs may circumvent CSS / AACS to make preservation or replacement copies of damaged or deteriorating DVDs/Blu-ray discs when no fairly-priced replacement or streaming alternative is available.
exemptions.evolution_notes: Recently introduced class (2021) addressing the gap left when commercial streaming/download services either do not offer motion pictures to LAMs or do so on unfavorable terms. Conditions include damage/deterioration of the source and reasonable-effort showing of no commercial alternative.

exemptions.name: Software preservation by LAMs (non-game programs)
exemptions.summary: Eligible LAMs may circumvent TPMs on lawfully acquired computer programs (excluding video games) no longer reasonably available commercially, for lawful preservation. Offsite single-user electronic lending permitted from 2021 onward.

2021.notes: Adds explicit permission for offsite electronic distribution to ONE USER AT A TIME, for a limited time, where LAM has no notice of non-private-study use

2024.notes: Adds explicit 'one user at a time' definition clarifying that a LAM with multiple lawfully owned copies may lend different copies to different users simultaneously

partial_denials.topic: Proposed Class 6(a) — remove the single-user limitation on software preservation entirely
partial_denials.reason_quote: The Register concludes that proponents did not show that removing the single-user limitation for preserved computer programs or permitting off-premises access to video games are likely to be noninfringing.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Distinct from the legacy obsolete-format-programs class (2003-2006) in user class (LAMs only) and source criterion ('no longer reasonably available' vs. 'obsolete format'). The 2021 expansion to offsite single-user lending and the 2024 clarification of 'one user at a time' both move toward 'controlled digital lending' models for preserved software.

exemptions.name: Video games — preservation when server abandoned (+ offline games by LAMs from 2018)
exemptions.summary: When a video game's authentication server has been abandoned, individual owners may restore local-gameplay access on PC/console; eligible LAMs may also preserve such games. From 2018 onward, LAMs may preserve offline-playable games no longer commercially available.

2018.notes: Adds subpart (ii) for preservation of offline games no longer reasonably available commercially (server-failure no longer required); expands 'complete games' definition for LAM preservation to include hybrid local/server games

partial_denials.topic: Proposed Class 14(b) — off-premises LAM access to preserved video games
partial_denials.reason_quote: With respect to video games, the Register concluded that proponents failed to carry their burden to show that the uses are likely noninfringing.

partial_denials.topic: Proposed Class 6(b) — remove video-game preservation's on-premises limitation
partial_denials.reason_quote: She also notes the greater risk of market harm with removing the video game exemption's premises limitation, given the market for legacy video games.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Originally tied to server-authentication failure (2015), then expanded in 2018 to cover any complete game no longer commercially available — a meaningful expansion of LAM preservation rights. 2021 and 2024 carried this forward unchanged.

exemptions.name: DRM authentication server shutdown (broad — beyond video games)
exemptions.summary: Proposal to permit circumvention when a DRM authentication server is shut down, broadly applied to all works (not just video games). DENIED in 2010 — proponent did not sustain burden of showing adverse effect. The video-game-specific version of this idea was later GRANTED in 2015 (video-games-preservation class).

2010.reason_quote: The Register cannot recommend this proposed class for the simple reason that the proponent has not sustained his burden of demonstrating that the prohibition on circumvention of access controls either has produced, or is likely to produce, any adverse effects on noninfringing uses of the proposed class of works.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Conceptual precursor to the granted video-games-preservation class. The broad cross-work proposal was denied in 2010, but a narrower video-game-server-shutdown petition succeeded in 2015.

exemptions.name: Library-distributed audiobooks (electronic audio format)
exemptions.summary: Proposal to permit library users to circumvent TPMs on electronically-distributed audiobooks. DENIED in 2006 — the complaint was about software incompatibility, not access controls; the technology in question was held to be 'use-facilitating' rather than 'access-controlling'.

2006.reason_quote: the commenter did not identify any technological measures that control access to the literary content of the digital books, nor does it explain how such measures are creating problems for users.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Single-cycle denial. The broader literary-works accessibility class (granted continuously since 2003) addresses some adjacent concerns.

exemptions.name: Wireless devices — unlocking to connect to a different carrier
exemptions.summary: Circumvent firmware/software locks that bind a wireless device to one carrier's network, to connect the device to a different network where that operator authorizes the connection. Scope has varied across cycles (used vs. new devices; phones only vs. tablets/hotspots/wearables; specific vs. any wireless device).

2010.notes: Restricted to 'used' handsets — those previously activated on a network

2012.notes: Further narrowed: only handsets acquired within 90 days of the rule's effective date, with conditions on carrier's failure to unlock

2015.notes: Device classes broadened: cellphones, tablets, mobile hotspots, wearables — all 'used' devices

2018.notes: Used-device requirement DROPPED — any lawfully acquired device of the covered classes qualifies

2021.notes: Device-class enumeration DROPPED — any wireless device qualifies

exemptions.evolution_notes: A particularly complex history. Narrowed twice (2010, 2012) under industry pressure, then broadened three times in succession (2015, 2018, 2021) — culminating in the simplest possible formulation in 2021. Reflects the policy shift from carrier-controlled unlocking to user-controlled unlocking that mirrored federal legislation (Unlocking Consumer Choice and Wireless Competition Act of 2014).

exemptions.name: Smartphones & portable mobile devices — jailbreaking (+ removal of software)
exemptions.summary: Circumvent OS-level TPMs on smartphones and similar devices to install lawfully obtained third-party software (interoperability) and, from 2015 onward, to remove software installed by the manufacturer or carrier.

2010.notes: The original 'iPhone class' — limited to handsets, interoperability only

2012.notes: Renewed; the Register declined to extend it to tablets in this cycle

partial_denials.topic: Proposed extension of jailbreaking exemption to tablets (later granted in 2015)
partial_denials.reason_quote: The Register determined that the record lacked a sufficient basis to develop an appropriate definition for the 'tablet' category of devices, a necessary predicate to extending the exemption beyond smartphones.

2015.notes: Adds 'portable all-purpose mobile computing devices' (tablet-like devices) AND adds removal-of-software clause

exemptions.evolution_notes: Has been granted in every cycle since 2010. Major expansion in 2015 to cover tablets/mobile computing devices generally and to permit software removal (carrier bloatware, etc.). Stable since 2015.

exemptions.name: Smart televisions — jailbreaking (interoperability only)
exemptions.summary: Circumvent TPMs on smart TVs to install lawfully obtained third-party software, for interoperability with on-device programs. Notably narrower than smartphone jailbreaking: no removal-of-software clause.

2021.notes: Definition of 'smart televisions' broadened to include devices physically separate from a TV whose primary purpose is to stream authorized video — i.e., set-top streaming boxes like Roku/AppleTV/Chromecast

exemptions.evolution_notes: Granted in 2015 with deliberately narrower scope than smartphone jailbreaking (no software-removal clause, reflecting concerns about ACR/advertising removal). The 2021 expansion to include separate streaming devices was a notable broadening.

exemptions.name: Voice assistant devices — jailbreaking (+ removal of software)
exemptions.summary: Circumvent TPMs on voice-input devices designed for home/office (e.g., smart speakers) to install lawfully obtained applications and to remove software, subject to the standard 'not for unauthorized access to other works' caveat.
exemptions.evolution_notes: Three consecutive cycles (2018, 2021, 2024). Stable since first granted.

exemptions.name: Routers & dedicated network devices — jailbreaking (interoperability only)
exemptions.summary: Circumvent TPMs on routers and dedicated network devices (switches, hubs, bridges, gateways, modems, repeaters, access points) to install lawfully obtained third-party software for interoperability.
exemptions.evolution_notes: Recently introduced (2021) class enabling third-party firmware (OpenWrt, DD-WRT, etc.) on network devices. Narrower than smartphone jailbreaking: no removal-of-software clause.

exemptions.name: Video game console jailbreaking
exemptions.summary: Proposal to permit jailbreaking of video game consoles for software interoperability (parallel to the granted smartphone class). DENIED in 2012 and 2015 — the Register has consistently held that console jailbreaking strongly correlates with piracy, unlike smartphone jailbreaking.

2012.reason_quote: Because the Register determined that the evidentiary record failed to support a finding that the inability to circumvent access controls on video game consoles has, or over the course of the next three years likely would have, a substantial adverse impact on the ability to make noninfringing uses, the Register declined to recommend the proposed class.

2015.reason_quote: jailbreaking of video game consoles continues to be closely associated with video game piracy.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Two consecutive denials (2012, 2015). The Register's piracy-correlation reasoning has been consistent. Not re-petitioned since 2015. NB: The 2021/2024 codified consumer-device repair class (b)(14)/(b)(15) includes a narrow video-game-console carve-out for optical-drive repair only, not for jailbreaking.

exemptions.name: E-book reader jailbreaking
exemptions.summary: Proposal to permit jailbreaking of dedicated e-book readers (Kindle, Nook, etc.) for software interoperability. DENIED in 2015 — proponent did not provide sufficient factual or legal support.

2015.reason_quote: In light of the insufficiency of factual or legal support for the proposed exemption, the Register declined to recommend it.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Single-cycle denial. Not re-petitioned.

exemptions.name: Personal computers / OS-restricted programs / secure boot
exemptions.summary: Proposals to permit circumvention of access controls on general-purpose personal computers, OS-locked computer programs, or secure-boot mechanisms. DENIED in 2006 (for OS-restricted programs) and 2012 (for the broad PC/secure-boot proposal) — insufficient evidence in both cases.

2006.reason_quote: The brief comments submitted on this issue failed to present sufficient evidence from which to conclude that technological measures that control access to works are interfering with the ability of users of copyrighted works to make noninfringing uses.

2012.reason_quote: Proponents had relied heavily on speculation and failed to present specific and compelling evidence in support of a focused exemption.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Two non-consecutive denials. PC jailbreaking has effectively never been on the table — partly because most PCs don't enforce OS lock-in the way mobile devices do.

exemptions.name: Motorized land vehicles (+ marine vessels from 2021) — diagnosis, repair, lawful modification
exemptions.summary: Circumvent ECU and other vehicle/vessel computer programs to diagnose, repair, or lawfully modify vehicle functions. Excludes subscription-service programs. Expanded to marine vessels in 2021.

2015.notes: Original scope: personal automobile, commercial motor vehicle, mechanized agricultural vehicle; excludes telematics/entertainment programs; 12-month delayed effective date

2018.notes: Excludes subscription-service programs (narrower exclusion than 2015's telematics/entertainment carve-out); 12-month delay DROPPED

2021.notes: Coverage adds 'marine vessels' (personal boats, commercial vessels, mechanized agricultural vessels)

exemptions.evolution_notes: Right-to-repair anchor class. Heavily contested in 2015 — initially saddled with a 12-month delay and broad telematics/entertainment carve-out. 2018 and 2021 successively expanded the scope (delay removed, exclusion narrowed, marine vessels added).

exemptions.name: Vehicles & marine vessels — owner access to operational/diagnostic/telematics data
exemptions.summary: Circumvent vehicle/vessel computer programs to allow owners and lessees (or their agents) to access, store, and share operational data including diagnostic and telematics data. Distinct from (and complementary to) the vehicle-repair class.
exemptions.evolution_notes: Newest exemption (2024) reflecting consumer/farmer pressure on access to vehicle-generated data — particularly important for independent repair shops and agricultural-equipment owners who otherwise rely on manufacturer-controlled data flows.

exemptions.name: Consumer devices — diagnosis, maintenance, or repair
exemptions.summary: Circumvent device computer programs to allow diagnosis, maintenance, or repair. First granted in 2018 for smartphones / home appliances / home systems; broadened in 2021 to any device 'primarily designed for use by consumers'. Includes a narrow carve-out for video game consoles (optical-drive repair only).

2018.notes: Limited to 'smartphone or home appliance or home system' (e.g., refrigerator, thermostat, HVAC, electrical system)

2021.notes: Broadened to any 'device primarily designed for use by consumers'; adds video-game-console carve-out (optical-drive repair only, requires TPM restoration)

partial_denials.topic: Proposed Class 5 (broader scope) — repair of all software-enabled commercial and industrial equipment (only the narrow retail food-prep subset was granted as (b)(16))
partial_denials.reason_quote: However, she declines to recommend an exemption for a broader class of software-enabled commercial and industrial devices in the absence of a sufficient showing of adverse effects on the record presented in this rulemaking.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Major right-to-repair class. The 2021 expansion from a defined-list scope to a general-consumer-device scope was one of the most significant single-cycle expansions in §1201 history. 2024 partial denial: broader commercial/industrial-equipment expansion was rejected; only the narrow retail food-prep subset (a separately-tracked class) was granted.

exemptions.name: Medical devices & systems — diagnosis, maintenance, or repair
exemptions.summary: Circumvent computer programs (and related data files) controlling lawfully acquired medical devices or systems, when necessary for diagnosis, maintenance, or repair. Distinct from medical-device-data (patient access to own data).
exemptions.evolution_notes: Established in 2021, distinct from consumer-device repair (because medical devices are not 'primarily designed for use by consumers'). Allows independent service providers and hospital biomedical-engineering teams to repair medical devices.

exemptions.name: Retail commercial food prep equipment — diagnosis, maintenance, or repair
exemptions.summary: Circumvent computer programs controlling lawfully acquired commercial food-prep equipment (e.g., commercial dishwashers, ice machines, ovens, soft-serve machines) when necessary for diagnosis, maintenance, or repair.
exemptions.evolution_notes: Newest right-to-repair class (2024). Targets the well-known problem of franchise/restaurant equipment (e.g., McDonald's ice cream machines) that can only be diagnosed/repaired through manufacturer-controlled software.

exemptions.name: Commercial & industrial equipment repair (beyond food prep)
exemptions.summary: Proposal to permit repair of all software-enabled commercial and industrial equipment (e.g., construction, manufacturing, retail machinery). DENIED in 2024 — Register granted only the narrow retail-food-prep subset (codified as (b)(16)) and declined the broader scope for lack of record.

2024.reason_quote: she declines to recommend an exemption for a broader class of software-enabled commercial and industrial devices in the absence of a sufficient showing of adverse effects on the record presented in this rulemaking.
2024.notes: Partial grant in same cycle: retail commercial food-prep equipment was carved out and granted as new class (b)(16) — tracked under exemption 'food-prep-equipment-repair'.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Likely to recur in future cycles as right-to-repair advocacy expands beyond consumer devices. The 2024 record was thin on commercial/industrial use cases beyond food prep.

exemptions.name: Medical-device data — patient access to own data
exemptions.summary: Patients (or persons acting on their behalf, from 2021 onward) may circumvent TPMs on data compilations generated by their own medical devices or personal monitoring systems, to access that data. Implantation requirement removed in 2021.

2015.notes: Limited to wholly/partially implanted medical devices and their personal monitoring systems; required 'passive monitoring of wireless transmissions already being produced'; patient personally must undertake circumvention

2021.notes: Multiple substantial expansions: 'by or on behalf of' a patient (delegation permitted); 'medical devices' broadly (implantation requirement removed); 'passive monitoring' restriction REMOVED

exemptions.evolution_notes: Hugo Campos's class — initially highly restricted (implanted devices only, patient must do the work themselves, passive monitoring only). 2021 expansions were transformative: any medical device, any agent of the patient, any access method permitted. Stable in 2024.

exemptions.name: 3D printers — feedstock / material interoperability
exemptions.summary: Circumvent TPMs that limit a 3D printer to manufacturer-approved feedstock/material, to allow use of alternative material. Excludes accessing design software/files/data.

2015.notes: Initially limited to 'microchip-reliant' TPMs and excluded 3D printers producing 'goods or materials for use in commerce' subject to regulatory oversight

2021.notes: 'Microchip-reliant' qualifier DROPPED; 'feedstock' generalized to 'material' — any TPM-limited material is now covered

exemptions.evolution_notes: Originally a tightly-scoped niche exemption (2015). Has been broadened in two consecutive renewals (2018, 2021) — first by dropping the regulated-commerce exclusion, then by removing the microchip-reliant and feedstock-specific framings.

exemptions.name: FOSS programs — investigation of potential license infringement
exemptions.summary: Circumvent TPMs on a lawfully acquired device (other than a video game console) to investigate potential infringement of free and open source software licenses, by parties with standing to bring a license breach or copyright infringement claim.
exemptions.evolution_notes: Niche but novel class (2021) enabling FOSS license enforcement (typically GPL compliance investigations) against device manufacturers who bundle FOSS into firmware and may be violating copyleft terms. Standing requirement and 'no facilitation of copyright infringement' conditions sharply limit who can use it.

exemptions.name: Broad use-based exemptions ('all fair use', 'all noninfringing uses')
exemptions.summary: Recurring proposal: a blanket exemption covering all works for noninfringing or fair uses. Repeatedly DENIED on procedural / substantive grounds — §1201's structure requires defining a class of works by qualities of the work itself, not by use or user. The Register has been consistent across cycles: this is the single most-rejected category of proposals.

2000.reason_quote: 'a particular class of work' must be determined primarily by reference to qualities of the work itself. It cannot be defined by reference to the class of users or uses of the work.

2003.reason_quote: the proponents of an exemption for 'all works' have utterly failed to propose 'a particular class of copyrighted works,' but have simply asked, in effect, for a blanket exemption for all works.

2006.reason_quote: These commenters have not articulated a sufficient class or provided sufficient evidence of adverse effects by the prohibition on noninfringing uses that would allow the articulation of a cognizable class.

2012.reason_quote: The Register concluded that the requested exemption to access public domain works was beyond the scope of the rulemaking proceeding and declined to recommend its adoption.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Petitioned and denied in four cycles (2000, 2003, 2006, 2012). Each denial articulated the same threshold doctrine: §1201(a)(1)(C) requires a class defined by reference to qualities of the work, not by purpose or user. After 2012, sophisticated petitioners stopped framing proposals this way — though the recurring petitions for things like 'all fair use works' before that reflected a persistent advocacy strategy that simply did not match the statute.

exemptions.name: Public-domain works behind TPMs
exemptions.summary: Petition to permit circumvention of TPMs on works in the public domain. DENIED multiple cycles on a particular threshold ground: §1201's prohibition on circumvention does not apply to works that are not copyrighted, so no exemption is needed.

2003.reason_quote: if a work that is entirely in the public domain is protected by an access control measure, the prohibition on circumvention will not be applicable. Therefore, no exemption is needed.

2006.reason_quote: The Register cannot recommend adoption of an exemption for this proposed class because it does not involve access controls and, therefore, no exemption is needed.

2012.reason_quote: The Register concluded that the requested exemption to access public domain works was beyond the scope of the rulemaking proceeding and declined to recommend its adoption.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Curious recurring petition. The Register's position is doctrinally clean (and arguably correct): §1201 only prohibits circumventing TPMs that effectively control access to copyrighted works. But the practical problem — TPMs sometimes do lock up public-domain content as a side effect of locking up copyrighted content — has not been addressed in the rulemaking.

exemptions.name: Avionics / aircraft data systems
exemptions.summary: Proposal to permit circumvention of access controls on aircraft electronic systems to enable access to flight/operations/maintenance/security data. DENIED in 2018 — the data at issue (flight statistics, fuel economy, etc.) are facts, which are not copyrightable, so §1201 does not apply.

2018.reason_quote: the data collected by aircrafts at issue consist of facts, which are not copyrightable. ... proponents have not alleged that the data or data compilations they are seeking to access are copyrightable, and thus subject to the prohibition on circumvention.

exemptions.evolution_notes: Single-cycle denial on a clean copyrightability ground. The proponent (Air Informatics) did not return in 2021 or 2024.
